summary: Describes the Internet Numbers Registry System used to hand out globally unique IP address space and autonomous system numbers, and the processes for evolving it. It documents how the system works today without proposing changes. It replaces RFC 2050.

eli5.summary: Like a phone book system, it explains who hands out the unique numbers that let every network and computer on the internet be found.

questions: what is the internet numbers registry system
subtitle: How IP addresses and AS numbers are allocated and managed globally.

tldr.problem: The global system that allocates unique IP addresses and autonomous system numbers is complex, with multiple levels of registries and policies; this needs to be documented.
tldr.mechanism: A hierarchical registry system runs from IANA at the top through Regional Internet Registries (RIRs) to Local Internet Registries (LIRs) and end users. The IETF sets technical standards and the ICANN community develops policies.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7020 documents the current system without proposing changes, providing a foundation for understanding Internet address governance. It replaces RFC 2050.

sections.title: The Address Allocation System
sections.content:
Every computer and network on the Internet needs a unique identifier. The Internet Numbers Registry System is the framework that assigns and tracks globally unique IP addresses and Autonomous System (AS) numbers.

RFC 7020 describes how this system works today, documenting it for future reference. It replaces RFC 2050 (which was issued in 1996) and reflects the significant changes that have occurred in the registry system since then. The RFC does not propose changes to the system; it simply describes the current state.
sections.eli5: Every internet address and network number needs to be different so networks can find each other. This document explains who hands these out and how they do it.

sections.title: Three Goals of the System
sections.content:
The Internet Numbers Registry System operates under three guiding goals:

Allocation Pool Management: Since IP addresses and AS numbers have fixed-length formats, the pools of available numbers are finite. Allocations must be made carefully to meet current operational needs while respecting future limitations.

Hierarchical Allocation: IP addresses are distributed hierarchically to support Internet routing aggregation. This hierarchical structure helps the routing system scale as the Internet grows.

Registration Accuracy: The registry system must maintain accurate records of all allocations to ensure uniqueness (no two parties get the same number) and to provide reliable information for operational requirements such as reverse DNS and WHOIS lookups.

These goals sometimes conflict with each other or with the interests of specific users and providers. Resolving these conflicts requires careful analysis and cooperation among all participants via community-developed policies.
sections.eli5: Three rules guide the system: there are only so many numbers, so use them wisely; organize them in a tree so routing works well; and keep honest records so nobody gets the same number twice.

sections.title: The Registry Hierarchy
sections.content:
The Internet Numbers Registry System is structured as a four-level hierarchy:

IETF: Sets the technical standards and specifications for IP addresses and AS numbers. The IETF also reserves portions of number space for future use and special purposes.

IANA: The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority, currently operated by ICANN, manages the top of the allocation hierarchy. IANA receives allocations and distributes them to Regional Internet Registries. IANA also develops allocation policies in coordination with the RIRs.

Regional Internet Registries (RIRs): Five continent-sized organizations that receive allocations from IANA and distribute them within their regions. Current RIRs are AfriNIC (Africa), APNIC (Asia-Pacific), ARIN (North America and Caribbean), LACNIC (Latin America and Caribbean), and RIPE NCC (Europe, Middle East, parts of Asia).

Local Internet Registries (LIRs): Organizations that receive allocations from RIRs (or parent LIRs) and distribute them to their customers, which may include ISPs, end users, or sub-LIRs.
sections.eli5: IETF says what kind of numbers we need. IANA has the master pile at the top. Five regional offices split it up by continent. Then local offices in each region hand them out to the ISPs and other customers.

sections.title: Technical Considerations
sections.content:
The registry system's operation is shaped by technical and operational requirements:

Reverse DNS: The registry system coordinates with the reverse DNS zone delegation process (managed by IANA) to ensure that network operators can properly set up reverse lookups for their address space.

WHOIS: Public WHOIS services allow network operators, security analysts, and others to query registry data about address allocations and their operators. The registry system maintains WHOIS as a key operational tool.

As the Internet and the registry system continue to evolve, the community examines these technical requirements and considers how to best meet them in the future.
sections.eli5: Two important tools depend on the registry system: reverse DNS (so emails have the right sender information) and WHOIS (so people can find out who runs a network).

sections.title: Future Evolution
sections.content:
The Internet Numbers Registry System is designed to evolve as the Internet community's needs change. Evolution happens through an open, transparent, multi-stakeholder process that respects the ICANN framework and core values.

Per the IETF/IAB/ICANN Memorandum of Understanding, discussions about the structure, policy, and processes of the registry system take place within the ICANN framework. These discussions must continue to consider the overall Internet address architecture and the technical goals of the registry system.

The IETF retains responsibility for non-policy aspects of Internet addressing, such as the architectural definition of address and AS number spaces and the technical goals and constraints associated with them. This division of responsibility allows technical standards development and address policy development to proceed in appropriate forums.
sections.eli5: The system changes as needed, but only through agreement by many people. The IETF handles the technical parts, while the ICANN community handles the policies about who gets what.
